paragraphs: Steerable convolutional networks encode geometric symmetries by restricting their weights. These restrictions make the network respond consistently to transformations, but they can become too restrictive when the relevant symmetries are unknown or vary within the data. This paper develops a way to learn how much equivariance the network should have, instead of fixing that choice in advance.

The method represents the degree of equivariance through a probability-based distribution over transformations. Fourier coefficients parameterize that distribution, and regularization makes the learned degree of equivariance interpretable across the network. The framework supports either separate choices for individual layers or a shared choice. It can learn equivariance to any subgroup of a compact group without adding extra layers.

Experiments on datasets containing mixed symmetries show competitive performance. The learned distributions also reflect the underlying degree of equivariance, providing insight into which symmetry constraints suit the data. The contribution therefore combines adaptable constraints with an interpretable account of the symmetry structure learned by the network.
icml-2024-a-probabilistic-approach-to-le.tldr: A probabilistic method lets steerable CNNs learn interpretable degrees of equivariance instead of imposing fixed symmetry constraints.

paragraphs: Active feature acquisition asks which information a model should obtain next when collecting information has a cost. The goal is to acquire a useful subset of features while maintaining accurate inference. In health care, for example, an additional measurement can carry costs in time, money, or risk that must be weighed against its expected diagnostic value.

The paper introduces the acquisition conditioned oracle, or ACO, a nonparametric approach to this sequential decision problem. It targets difficulties faced by existing approaches: reinforcement learning policies can be hard to train over complex decision spaces, while generative approaches must model complicated conditional distributions. Greedy methods face a different problem: features that are informative together may be overlooked when evaluated one at a time.

The authors report extensive experiments in which ACO outperforms state-of-the-art methods for acquiring features for prediction and broader decision-making. Its significance is a nongreedy route that bypasses many of those modeling and training challenges while accounting for the value of information acquired jointly.
icml-2024-acquisition-conditioned-oracle.tldr: ACO uses a nonparametric oracle approach to choose informative feature acquisitions beyond greedy decisions.

paragraphs: Event-based sensors generate sparse streams of changes across space and time, creating a mismatch with dense machine learning models. ALERT-Transformer addresses this mismatch by separating continuous updates from the timing of downstream processing. Its pipeline combines asynchronous sensing with synchronous computation so that conventional models can work with features representing the current event stream.

The central ALERT module uses a PointNet-based embedding that continuously incorporates incoming events. A leakage mechanism removes the influence of older events. A flexible readout then supplies updated features whenever a downstream model needs them, at a chosen sampling rate. The pipeline also uses a patch-based design inspired by Vision Transformers to exploit sparsity and improve computational efficiency.

The authors feed these embeddings into a transformer trained for object and gesture recognition. They report state-of-the-art performance with lower latency than competing methods and demonstrate operation at arbitrary desired sampling rates. The approach matters because it lets the event representation evolve continuously while leaving the timing of downstream decisions flexible.
icml-2024-alert-transformer-bridging-asy.tldr: ALERT-Transformer continuously embeds sparse sensor events for flexible downstream processing, achieving state-of-the-art recognition with lower latency.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to maintain attention outputs when the matrices used by attention change incrementally. In its formal setting, each update changes one entry of the key or value matrix. A later query asks for one particular entry of the normalized attention output. The focus is the computational cost of supporting these operations over time.

The proposed data structure uses lazy updates and offers a tradeoff controlled by a parameter tau between zero and one. Its amortized update time is O(n^(omega(1,1,tau)−tau)), and its worst-case query time is O(n^(1+tau)). Here omega describes the exponent for the relevant rectangular matrix multiplication. Amortized update cost describes cost averaged across operations, whereas the query guarantee applies to each query.

The authors also establish a conditional barrier to improving both costs simultaneously by polynomial factors. That barrier relies on the hinted matrix-vector multiplication conjecture. Together, the algorithm and lower bound characterize a computational tradeoff for this specific dynamic attention problem; the impossibility result remains conditional on the conjecture.
icml-2024-algorithm-and-hardness-for-dyn.tldr: A lazy-update data structure supports dynamic attention queries with a tradeoff that is conditionally resistant to simultaneous polynomial improvements.

paragraphs: Speech recognition in a dialog system is often trained as though every utterance were an isolated event. That overlooks information available across an evolving conversation, including feedback from the user. This paper introduces a framework that lets the recognizer learn over time from multiple turns, using both explicit supervision and implicit conversational feedback.

The framework combines student-teacher learning with dialog processing that takes context into account. It also introduces contrastive self-supervision and an online hard-negative mining method called Ohm. These components provide a way to use conversational information as training signals, extending learning beyond independently labeled utterances. The aim is to improve recognition through interaction rather than treating each new turn as disconnected from previous ones.

Compared with traditional training, the authors report relative word error rate reductions close to 10% in real-world dialog systems and up to 26% on public synthetic data. These are relative reductions in recognition errors, not percentage-point gains in accuracy. The results support the practical value of incorporating context and feedback into speech recognition training.
icml-2024-an-efficient-self-learning-fra.tldr: A conversational self-learning framework improves speech recognition using context and feedback, reducing real-world word error rates by close to 10% relatively.

paragraphs: Vision-language models can recognize categories without task-specific training, but successful recognition does not automatically make their confidence estimates trustworthy. This paper studies calibration: whether a model's expressed confidence corresponds to how often it is correct. That distinction matters when uncertainty estimates help determine how much to rely on a prediction.

The authors examine different architectures, datasets, and training strategies. They specifically test what happens when calibration is performed in one domain, with one label set, or at one level of a label hierarchy, and the model is evaluated under different conditions. This makes the study relevant to situations where the available calibration examples do not exactly match subsequent use.

The experiments find that vision-language models are not inherently calibrated, but temperature scaling significantly and consistently improves their calibration. Improvements persist across distribution shifts and changes in the label set, and calibration can work with very few examples. These findings support a relatively simple route toward more reliable confidence estimates under the changes examined in the study.
icml-2024-an-empirical-study-into-what-m.tldr: Temperature scaling consistently improves vision-language model calibration, including across tested distribution and label-set changes.

paragraphs: When a user edits text produced by a language model, the edit contains information about what that user prefers. It may still be imperfect, making it unsuitable as an unquestioned target for supervised training. This paper instead treats the edit as a relative signal: the revised text is assumed to improve on the model's original proposal.

The authors develop a theoretical foundation for applying this coactive learning idea to nonlinear models and derive an algorithm called CoRLL for language models. Its learning signal comes from the preference between the original and edited versions, rather than requiring the revision to be a gold-standard answer. Because edits can be associated with individual users, this mechanism also creates an opportunity for personalization.

Empirical results indicate that CoRLL remains effective when coactive preference feedback is weak and noisy. The findings make naturally occurring edits a promising source of training data. The central assumption is comparative improvement: the method draws value from a revision being better than its starting point, even if it remains far from ideal.
icml-2024-coactive-learning-for-large-la.tldr: CoRLL trains and personalizes language models from user edits treated as improvements rather than perfect target answers.

paragraphs: Time-series causal discovery often assumes that all observations arise from one underlying causal model. Heterogeneous data can violate that assumption: different samples may reflect different relationships between variables. This paper develops MCD, a framework for discovering a mixture of causal models instead of forcing every sample into a shared causal structure.

MCD uses variational inference to learn the underlying models together with each sample's mixing probabilities. Training proceeds jointly by maximizing a lower bound on the data likelihood. The authors provide two versions with different modeling choices. MCD-Linear handles linear causal relationships and independent noise, while MCD-Nonlinear allows nonlinear relationships and noise that depends on the preceding history.

Experiments on synthetic and real-world data show improvements over state-of-the-art causal discovery benchmarks, particularly when samples originate from different causal graphs. The authors also prove identifiability under stated mild assumptions, giving theoretical support for recovering the mixture structure. The contribution connects heterogeneous time-series modeling with causal discovery while retaining explicit assumptions about when the model can be identified.
icml-2024-discovering-mixtures-of-struct.tldr: MCD jointly learns multiple causal models and sample mixing probabilities from heterogeneous time series, with conditional identifiability guarantees.

paragraphs: People decide when to use a language model partly by extrapolating from its previous successes and failures. A good answer on one task may encourage them to trust it on another. This paper studies that extrapolation as a human generalization function, connecting model evaluation to the beliefs that shape actual deployment decisions.

The authors collect 19,000 examples of human generalizations across 79 tasks from MMLU and BIG-Bench. They find that NLP methods can predict these judgments, suggesting that people's expectations follow consistent patterns. They then evaluate how well language model performance aligns with those expectations, rather than considering capability independently of the tasks people choose to delegate.

The results show that more capable models, including GPT-4, can perform worse on the instances people select for them when performance does not align with human generalization. This issue is especially pronounced when mistakes are costly. The finding makes user expectations part of the evaluation problem: broader capability alone does not guarantee better outcomes under human-directed use.
icml-2024-do-large-language-models-perfo.tldr: More capable language models can fare worse on human-selected tasks when their abilities diverge from users' expectations.

paragraphs: Partial monitoring studies repeated decisions made with limited feedback. A learner must choose how to explore even when observations do not directly reveal everything needed to judge its actions. Exploration by optimization provides strong guarantees against adversarial environments, but applying it naively in stochastic environments leads to substantially weaker regret bounds.

This paper introduces an exploration-by-optimization framework with a hybrid regularizer for locally observable games. It improves best-of-both-worlds guarantees, which aim to perform nearly optimally in both stochastic and adversarial settings. The stochastic regret bound sums k²m² log(T)/Delta_a over suboptimal actions, where k counts actions, m counts observations, T counts rounds, and Delta_a measures each action's disadvantage relative to an optimum.

The authors describe this bound as roughly a factor of k² log(T) smaller than existing best-of-both-worlds bounds. They also give a new algorithm for globally observable games with the first logarithmic-in-T stochastic bound of this kind. The results strengthen performance in stochastic environments while preserving adversarial robustness within the game classes studied.
icml-2024-exploration-by-optimization-wi.tldr: Hybrid regularization improves stochastic regret guarantees for partial monitoring while retaining best-of-both-worlds adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: A diffusion model can represent a broad distribution while rarely producing the particular samples a user wants. The desired samples might have high aesthetic quality or strong biological activity. This paper frames adaptation toward such properties as reinforcement learning, with a reward function specifying what makes a generated sample valuable.

Having access to the true reward through online queries does not by itself make the search efficient. High-reward samples may initially be rare, and some generated candidates may be infeasible, leaving their rewards undefined. The proposed reinforcement learning procedure addresses this difficulty by exploring on the manifold of feasible samples, directing the search toward the part of the sample space where meaningful evaluation is possible.

The authors provide a theoretical regret guarantee and empirical validation on images, biological sequences, and molecules. The contribution is a feedback-efficient approach to improving generation under these exploration challenges. Its relevance extends across the tested domains because each requires finding desirable outputs within a space where feasibility and reward both matter.
icml-2024-feedback-efficient-online-fine.tldr: A reinforcement learning procedure fine-tunes diffusion models by efficiently exploring feasible samples in search of higher rewards.

paragraphs: Sharpness-aware minimization, or SAM, often improves generalization, yet the sharpness of its final models does not always track their generalization error. This paper proposes a different explanation based on the training process. Its central idea is perturbed forgetting: perturbations discard undesirable model biases and reveal learning signals that transfer better beyond the training data.

The authors connect this account to the information bottleneck principle and use it to explain observations such as the benefits of smaller perturbation batches. They show that their forgetting measure can correlate more strongly with generalization than flatness does. They also introduce perturbations targeting biases visible through model outputs, extending beyond the steepest-ascent directions used by standard SAM.

These output bias forgetting perturbations outperform SAM, GSAM, and ASAM on ImageNet, robustness benchmarks, and transfer to CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100. Some resulting solutions occupy sharper regions. The findings support an alternative mechanistic explanation of SAM's benefits in which improved generalization need not depend on reaching a flatter loss surface.
icml-2024-forget-sharpness-perturbed-for.tldr: The paper explains SAM through forgetting undesirable biases and introduces output-based perturbations that improve tested results, sometimes at sharper solutions.

paragraphs: Variational inequalities provide a mathematical framework for problems arising in adversarial and multi-agent learning. Many convergence analyses impose strong monotonicity and Lipschitz continuity, assumptions that do not hold in many machine learning settings. This paper studies a broader structured class by relaxing both the monotonicity and smoothness requirements used in such analyses.

The main technique is to adapt the stepsize as the algorithm progresses. The authors establish convergence results for three familiar approaches: projection, Korpelevich, and Popov methods. Their results cover generalized smooth variational inequalities, including the structured non-monotone setting they study. This expands the conditions under which these methods have theoretical support without claiming convergence for every non-monotone problem.

The resulting convergence rates match or improve existing rates for smooth variational inequalities. Numerical experiments support the guarantees and demonstrate the efficiency of the proposed adaptive stepsizes. The contribution is therefore both analytical and algorithmic: changing how step lengths are chosen allows useful convergence guarantees to extend beyond the more restrictive conventional assumptions.
icml-2024-generalized-smooth-variational.tldr: Adaptive stepsizes give three established variational inequality methods convergence guarantees under relaxed smoothness and monotonicity assumptions.

paragraphs: Antibody humanness is used as a proxy for the immune response that an antibody therapeutic might provoke. Such responses are a major obstacle in drug development and clinical use. This paper investigates whether information contained in patents can improve humanness prediction through a training process that combines multiple stages and objectives.

The first stage uses weakly supervised contrastive learning. Each antibody sequence can carry several identifiers describing its function, and the encoder learns to group sequences according to their patented properties. The authors then freeze part of this encoder and continue training on patent data with a cross-entropy objective to predict humanness scores. This connects representations of patented properties to the final prediction task.

Evaluation uses three immunogenicity datasets that were unseen during training. The learned model consistently outperforms the alternative baselines and achieves state-of-the-art results on five of six inference tasks across the metrics used. These results support the value of patent data for the prediction problem, while humanness remains a proxy for immunogenic response.
icml-2024-improving-antibody-humanness-p.tldr: Multistage learning from antibody patents improves humanness prediction, achieving state-of-the-art results on five of six evaluated inference tasks.

paragraphs: Forecasts arranged in a hierarchy must be accurate individually and consistent collectively: predictions for smaller groups should add up to the prediction for their parent group. Reconciliation adjusts forecasts to satisfy these relationships. This paper studies how to learn the projection used for reconciliation from data instead of selecting its matrix in advance.

The authors examine Euclidean and general oblique projections, then build reconciliation into a neural forecaster as a structured, learnable layer. An oblique projection can account for the hierarchy and give different weights to individual series, offering more adaptability than an orthogonal projection that treats base forecast errors equally. It also preserves unbiasedness. Training learns the forecasting model and its projection together in one end-to-end process.

Experiments on real-world hierarchical time series show better performance than existing state-of-the-art approaches. The significance is that coherence becomes part of the learned forecasting architecture. The model can adapt how it reconciles predictions while retaining the required relationships between levels, rather than relying on a projection fixed before training.
icml-2024-learning-optimal-projection-fo.tldr: A learnable projection layer jointly improves hierarchical forecasts and reconciles them so predictions add up consistently.

paragraphs: In a matroid semi-bandit problem, a learner repeatedly selects a feasible subset of available arms to maximize accumulated expected reward. When the number of arms is large, even choosing the next subset can be computationally expensive. This paper introduces FasterCUCB to reduce the cost of that selection step for several common matroid classes.

The method dynamically maintains an approximate maximum-weight basis with weights expressed through inner products. For uniform, partition, and graphical matroids, its sampling rule costs D times polylogarithmic factors in K and T. For transversal matroids, it costs D times the square root of K and a polylogarithmic factor in T. Here K is the number of arms, D the largest feasible subset size, and T the horizon.

Using an approximate basis makes the regret analysis more difficult, but the authors retain a bound as tight as CUCB's in the stated asymptotic, gap-dependent sense. It matches the corresponding lower bound asymptotically. The contribution combines faster selection with strong learning guarantees; the computational bounds explicitly retain their dependence on subset size.
icml-2024-matroid-semi-bandits-in-sublin.tldr: FasterCUCB reduces sampling costs for common matroids while retaining asymptotically tight gap-dependent regret guarantees.

paragraphs: Neurosymbolic systems combine neural predictions with logical constraints, often using probabilistic reasoning to connect the two. Many simplify this reasoning by assuming that symbols are conditionally independent once the input is given. This paper examines the consequences of that assumption for both learning and the ability to express uncertainty over logically valid predictions.

The authors prove that the studied loss functions push conditionally independent networks toward overconfident predictions. As a result, these networks cannot represent uncertainty across multiple valid options. This is a problem even when several answers satisfy the constraints: the learning formulation favors confidence rather than preserving the ambiguity among those acceptable possibilities.

The analysis also shows that the minima of these losses are usually highly disconnected and non-convex, making optimization difficult. The paper therefore identifies two linked costs of the simplifying assumption: distorted uncertainty and a challenging optimization landscape. Its theoretical results provide a foundation for replacing conditional independence with more expressive probabilistic models, rather than treating logical consistency alone as sufficient for reliable predictions.
icml-2024-on-the-independence-assumption.tldr: Theoretical analysis shows how conditional independence in neurosymbolic learning can induce overconfidence and difficult optimization landscapes.

paragraphs: Many matrix optimization problems require a generalized orthogonality constraint, written XᵀBX = I. The matrix B can represent a sampled covariance structure, connecting this setting to canonical correlation analysis, independent component analysis, and generalized eigenvalue problems. Conventional iterative methods typically need the full matrix B to carry out their updates.

This paper proposes a stochastic method that works with random estimates of B instead. It does not force every intermediate matrix to satisfy the constraint. Rather, its iterates converge to critical points on the generalized Stiefel manifold defined in expectation. Allowing intermediate violations avoids having to restore exact feasibility after every update and lets the method operate using only matrix multiplications.

The authors report lower per-iteration cost while retaining the convergence rates of Riemannian optimization counterparts that require the complete B matrix. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on the three application types discussed above. The result supports cheaper optimization with incomplete covariance information, with the stated convergence target being critical points rather than a guarantee of globally optimal solutions.
icml-2024-optimization-without-retractio.tldr: A stochastic matrix optimization method uses random estimates of B and approaches generalized orthogonality without enforcing it at every iteration.

paragraphs: Regression trees describe complex relationships through understandable branching decisions. Finding an optimal tree is NP-hard, so training usually relies on greedy choices. This paper works on optimal methods directly, developing dynamic programming approaches that make exact optimization more scalable for trees whose regions contain either constant or linear predictions.

There are three main contributions. A specialized algorithm for depth-two trees improves a piecewise constant regression tree method. A second approach provides the first optimal dynamic programming method for piecewise multiple linear regression. A third supplies the first optimal method for piecewise simple linear regression, also with a specialized depth-two algorithm. These approaches expand the kinds of predictive models that can be fitted optimally within tree regions.

Experiments show scalability improvements of at least one order of magnitude over state-of-the-art optimal methods, alongside similar or better out-of-sample performance. The results make optimal regression tree construction more practical in the tested settings. They also show that the computational gains need not come at the expense of predictive performance on unseen data.
icml-2024-piecewise-constant-and-linear-.tldr: New dynamic programming methods make optimal constant and linear regression trees substantially more scalable while preserving or improving tested predictive performance.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning research should devote more attention to foundation models for tabular data. The authors see an imbalance: text and image models attract increasing resources, while tables remain central to many fields but receive comparatively little attention and lag in model scale and capability.

They propose prioritizing Large Tabular Models, or LTMs. The central vision is to analyze a table in the context of related datasets instead of treating each dataset as an isolated problem. This shifts the ambition from building a separate model around each table toward models that can draw useful context from a broader collection of tabular information.

The authors describe potential benefits including learning from few examples, automating parts of data science, generating out-of-distribution synthetic data, and supporting discovery across disciplines. These are proposed opportunities, rather than demonstrated outcomes of a new system. The paper's contribution is a research agenda and an argument about resource allocation: tabular foundation models could have broad scientific and practical impact if developed successfully.
icml-2024-position-why-tabular-foundatio.tldr: This position paper calls for Large Tabular Models that contextualize individual tables using related datasets.

paragraphs: Differentially private stochastic gradient descent involves choices that jointly affect privacy, accuracy, and implementation. Privacy accountants usually track how much privacy budget training consumes. Proactive DP instead uses a fixed privacy budget to help choose training parameters in advance, with the goal of optimizing anticipated test accuracy alongside practical objectives.

The authors improve the moment accounting method and derive a closed-form privacy guarantee linking the training parameters. Their stated sufficient conditions connect noise, training rounds, dataset size, and gradient computations measured in epochs, within a specified privacy regime. They also show a form of near-tightness: reducing the number of rounds sufficiently below the stated threshold, by roughly a factor of four, violates the guarantee under their analysis.

The framework turns this theory into a utility graph and a DP calculator that search for experiment configurations satisfying multiple objectives. A full implementation flow and proof-of-concept experiments demonstrate the approach. The main benefit is planning: privacy becomes a constraint used to design a training setup, together with expected utility and implementation requirements.
icml-2024-proactive-dp-a-multiple-target.tldr: Proactive DP uses improved privacy accounting to select DP-SGD parameters in advance for a fixed privacy budget and anticipated utility.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates discovering an environment from deciding what to accomplish in it. First, an agent gathers trajectories without a predetermined reward function. Later, a reward is supplied, and the agent uses those earlier experiences to calculate a near-optimal policy. The challenge is to collect sufficiently useful information before knowing the eventual objective.

Previous algorithms and sample complexity guarantees cover tabular models, linear approximations, or very smooth function approximations. This paper expands the setting to a broad range of kernel-based approximations, including non-smooth kernels. Its proposed exploration algorithm uses adaptive domain partitioning, allowing the analysis to address function classes beyond those previously handled by the more restrictive approaches.

The authors prove order-optimal sample complexity for a large class of common kernels, including Matérn and Neural Tangent kernels. This describes how efficiently exploration data can support the subsequent planning stage within the covered classes. The contribution broadens the theoretical basis for reward-free exploration while retaining a strong guarantee on the amount of experience required.
icml-2024-reward-free-kernel-based-reinf.tldr: Adaptive domain partitioning enables reward-free reinforcement learning with order-optimal sample complexity for a broad class of kernels.

paragraphs: Simplicity bias describes a neural network's tendency to rely too heavily on simple features, potentially weakening its performance outside the training distribution. Earlier theoretical characterizations required restrictive dataset assumptions such as linear separability. This paper extends the analysis to general datasets for two-layer networks, while assuming small initial weights and training by gradient flow.

The authors prove that early in training, learned features gather around a small number of directions. Those directions do not depend on the hidden layer's size, so increasing width does not change this particular early clustering structure. For datasets with an XOR-like pattern, the analysis goes further: it identifies the learned features precisely and shows that simplicity bias becomes stronger later in training.

These results suggest that representations from intermediate training stages may transfer better to out-of-distribution data than later representations. Experiments on images support that hypothesis. The practical implication is about when useful features appear during learning, while the theoretical conclusions retain the specified network, initialization, and training assumptions.
icml-2024-simplicity-bias-of-two-layer-n.tldr: Under small initialization and gradient flow, two-layer networks develop clustered features, with results suggesting intermediate representations may transfer better.

paragraphs: A generative model should capture the distribution behind its training examples while producing diverse outputs. Measuring closeness to the true distribution addresses only part of that goal; it does not directly assess separation from the observed sample collection. This paper studies both questions mathematically, focusing on a constrained form of Wasserstein GAN.

The constraint requires the generator's push-forward map to be left-invertible, meaning it has an inverse on its outputs that recovers its input. Under the studied setup, the authors show that this restriction prevents replication and creates substantial separation from the empirical distribution without sacrificing statistical optimality. Their central result is a finite-sample lower bound on Wasserstein-1 distance from that empirical distribution.

A complementary upper bound controls distance from the true data-generating distribution. Both bounds explicitly reflect sample size, ambient and latent dimensions, noise, and Lipschitz smoothness. Together, they formalize how a generator can remain statistically accurate while differing from the observed sample distribution. The result concerns these mathematical notions of non-replication and accuracy under the stated generator constraint.
icml-2024-statistically-optimal-generati.tldr: Left-invertible Wasserstein GAN generators can separate from the empirical distribution without losing statistical optimality, as quantified by finite-sample bounds.

paragraphs: Neural architectures differ substantially, yet their learned representations can display similar qualitative patterns. This paper asks whether a shared description of representation learning can explain some of those similarities. It develops an effective theory intended for large, flexible architectures whose hidden representations are not strongly restricted by their particular parameterization.

The theory assumes that the map from inputs to hidden representations and the map from representations to outputs are arbitrary smooth functions. This abstraction shifts attention toward how representations evolve when architecture imposes relatively weak constraints. It is an account of a particular flexible-model regime, rather than a claim that architecture has no effect on what networks learn.

Experiments show that the theory captures aspects of learning dynamics across networks with different architectures and activation functions. It also displays phenomena resembling rich and lazy learning regimes. Although quantitative behavior still depends on architecture, the findings suggest that certain qualitative behaviors are widely shared once models have sufficient flexibility. The contribution is a common theoretical description of those conserved aspects.
icml-2024-when-representations-align-uni.tldr: An effective theory explains shared aspects of representation learning dynamics when neural architectures are sufficiently flexible.
